dimension: Volunteer and distributed computing work allocation — BOINC, SETI@home, Folding@home, Einstein@Home, HTCondor ClassAds, grid and desktop-grid scheduling, and peer-to-peer reciprocity
citations_that_failed: Cohen, IPTPS 2003 — WRONG VENUE. 'Incentives Build Robustness in BitTorrent' was presented at the Workshop on Economics of Peer-to-Peer Systems (P2PECON), Berkeley, 22 May 2003, not IPTPS. Verified against the paper PDF (cs.princeton.edu/courses/archive/fall14/cos561/papers/BitTorrent03.pdf) and the venue listing. The paper's content is otherwise correctly used: 'each BitTorrent peer always unchokes a fixed number of other peers (default is four)' and 'at all times a BitTorrent peer has a single optimistic unchoke' are both verbatim.

Elwaer et al., IPDPSW 2011 — WRONG VENUE. Anderson's own reference [45] in arXiv:1903.01699 gives it as 'IEEE Ninth International Symposium on Parallel and Distributed Processing with Applications Workshops, Busan, South Korea, 2011' (ISPA Workshops), not IPDPS Workshops. The quoted verdict is verbatim and correct: 'This method hasn't been used by any projects, but it may be useful in the future.'

CreditNew: 'is complicated and I'm not sure it ever worked exactly as I intended' — NO SOURCE LOCATED. The dimension attributes this to 'the designer's own verdict' with no citation at all. I checked the BOINC CreditNew wiki page (github.com/BOINC/boinc/wiki/CreditNew — no occurrence of 'complicated' or 'intended'), the full text of arXiv:1903.01699 (two matches for 'intended', neither about credit: 'BOINC is intended to be usable for computer owners...' and 'The original BOINC participation model was intended to result in...'), and the HICSS paper. The old trac CreditNew URL returns 404. My WebSearch budget was exhausted before I could search message-board archives, so I cannot call it fabricated — but it is UNVERIFIED and it is load-bearing: it is one of the three pillars of the dimension's 'NOT already invented' half. It must not be quoted to the founder until a URL is produced.

'Their journal abstract states that ranking desktop resources according to their clock rates ... is surprisingly effective' — MISATTRIBUTED TO THE WRONG PAPER. That sentence is in the abstract of the SC '04 CONFERENCE paper (Kondo, Chien, Casanova, 'Resource Management for Rapid Application Turnaround on Enterprise Desktop Grids'), verbatim: 'We find that ranking desktop resources according to their clock rates, without taking into account their availability history, is surprisingly effective in practice.' The journal paper exists and the pagination is right (Journal of Grid Computing vol 5, pp. 379-405, 2007, DOI 10.1007/s10723-007-9063-y, verified via Semantic Scholar), but its abstract is paywalled and I could not confirm the sentence appears there. Cite the SC '04 abstract.

Piatek et al., NSDI 2007 — QUOTE REVERSED BY OMISSION. 'Sufficiently low bandwidth peers almost never earn reciprocation' is verbatim (people.cs.umass.edu/~arun/papers/bittyrant.pdf, section 3.4). The NEXT TWO SENTENCES contradict the use the dimension makes of it: 'Note that low bandwidth peers, despite not being reciprocated, still receive data in aggregate faster than they send data. This is because they receive indiscriminate optimistic unchokes from other users in spite of their low upload capacity.' The paper's finding is that low-capacity peers are OVER-served, not starved. The dimension's fifth point ('the small-model end will be starved by the very mechanism intended to honour the heterogeneity constraint') is the opposite of what the cited source measured.

SETI@home, CACM 45(11) — TWO REAL QUOTES STITCHED TO A RATIONALE THE PAPER DOES NOT GIVE. 'never turn away a client asking for work' and 'revising the client to do more computation per work unit' are both verbatim, but they sit in one sentence about REDUNDANCY MANAGEMENT, not heterogeneity: because they never turn a client away, 'the redundancy level increases with the number of clients and their average speed ... We have kept the redundancy level within the desired range by revising the client to do more computation per work unit.' The dimension presents the work-unit enlargement as 'SETI@home's response to the same heterogeneity', which the source does not say. ('There is no communication between clients' is verbatim and correctly used.)

Estrada et al., e-Science '06 — 'MEASURED' IS NOT SUPPORTED. The paper NAMES starvation precisely: 'This policy has the disadvantage of starving workers that are considered to be unsuitable to perform the work at hand and, thus, virtually removes these workers from a project.' But it reports no measurement of it; the only adjacent empirical remark is 'During simulations we observed that the availability and reliability ratings of workers change slowly'. Also the starvation is a property of Estrada's OWN threshold-admission policy, not of BOINC host punishment, so it is not evidence 'that occurs without it [the quota floor]'. The other three Estrada claims are verbatim and correct: 'An available worker is not necessarily a reliable worker', 'Availability and reliability are not directly correlated', and the explicit Kondo disagreement attributed to 'The differences in the traces and the models of the computing environments'.
overstated_verdicts: ALL FIVE DIRECTLY_APPLICABLE verdicts fail the founder's no-central-coordinator constraint, and the dimension never propagates its own fourth disagreement back into the verdicts. Probe jobs store output 'in the host record in the database' (HICSS 4.9); proj_flops is 'maintained by the BOINC server' per (host, app version) (arXiv 6.3); job-size matching needs the size_census daemon to sort the whole population and the feeder to load quantiles into shared memory (JobSizeMatching wiki); adaptive replication and host punishment are both server-side counters. Every one is CONDITIONALLY_APPLICABLE at best under a hard no-coordinator constraint. The dimension states the conflict as a disagreement and then leaves five DIRECTLY_APPLICABLE labels standing.

proj_flops: the recommended cold start VIOLATES the founder's 'capability is measured, never a name' hard constraint, and the dimension does not notice. Only tier 1 of the three-tier ladder is measured. Tier 2 is the per-app-version population mean; tier 3 is 'the peak FLOPS of V running on H, i.e. the sum over processing resources R of V's usage of R times the peak FLOPS of R' — a DECLARED hardware spec. Plan classes, which gate app-version selection upstream, match on GPU model and driver version, i.e. on the device's name. The dimension's own advice — 'Route the first jobs using a cheap declared prior' — is routing by the spec sheet, which is the one thing the founder forbids. A verdict of DIRECTLY_APPLICABLE on a mechanism whose first roughly 10 samples per (seat, task type) run on a forbidden prior is overstated.

Probe jobs: 'already implemented, already wired to a scoring function' is stronger than the evidence. HICSS 4.9 says BOINC 'allows projects to provide' probe jobs and that the output 'can be referenced in a project-specific scoring function' — a capability a project must build, not a wired path. BOINC's current AssignedWork documentation lists only --broadcast, --broadcast_user, --broadcast_team, --target_host, --target_user, --target_team; it describes no probe-job type, no host-record output field, and notes broadcast jobs 'skip the validator and assimilator', so the project must supply its own daemon. Also, the paper's only example is a boolean presence check ('whether the client has a particular software package installed'), not a graded capability measurement. Finally, 'the probe runs on every participant on first contact, before any ordinary work is routed' is not in the source; the source says only 'executed exactly once on all hosts'.

proj_flops transfers the WRONG AXIS. It measures SPEED — the sample mean of runtime(J)/est_flop_count(J) — against a difficulty estimate 'supplied by the job submitter', and exists explicitly to absorb 'systematic error in est_flop_count()'. CDSFL has no est_flop_count analogue for a claim, and a seat's latency is close to uninformative about its falsification quality. The BOINC mechanism that tracks QUALITY is the adaptive-replication reputation stream, kept per (host, app version), not proj_flops. Calling proj_flops 'the strongest competitor to the founder's cold start' maps a quality problem onto a throughput estimator.

'His no-participant-is-ever-permanently-set-aside constraint is BOINC host punishment' holds only inside the pool that already passed the capability gate. The quota floor of 1 is confirmed verbatim ('a host who experiences nothing but errors will be eventually limited to only one job instance per day', with recovery by doubling, HICSS 4.10) — but it governs ERROR punishment only. The routing filter upstream is absolute: arXiv 6.4, 'If no such app version exists, we continue to the next job.' A host whose platform or plan class has no matching app version gets nothing, permanently, by declared capability. BOINC does not in general satisfy the founder's constraint.

The 'no field validation of any of it' pillar is 17 years stale and is refuted by two papers in the dimension's own citation set. 'However, we currently are unable to quantify how well they work' is verbatim from the HICSS conclusion — but the sentence before it reads 'These mechanism are operational on World Community Grid and other BOINC projects, and they seem to work', and the paragraph after it announces the simulator built to fix exactly this. That simulator was delivered: Anderson, 'Emulating Volunteer Computing Scheduling Policies' (PCGrid 2011), abstract: 'This system has been useful in the design and evaluation of policies, in software development, and in the resolution of problems occurring in the field.' And Estrada et al. (2006) evaluated threshold-admission policies on real Predictor@Home traces representing 340 hours via the SimBA discrete-event simulator. Trace-driven validation of this policy class exists; what does not exist is a controlled field A/B on a production project.

'A roster-wide capability ranking with no coordinator is NOT already invented' is falsified by a paper cited inside the dimension's own primary source for the claim. The Network of Favours paper's related-work section describes 'EigenRep [12] each peer stores local reputation values and in addition random peers store global values derived from multiple local values' — that is EigenTrust (Kamvar, Schlosser, Garcia-Molina, WWW '03, p. 640, DOI 10.1145/775152.775242), which computes a GLOBAL trust vector by distributed iteration with no central authority. The dimension read the NoF paper closely enough to get its pagination right (HPDC-13 2004, pp. 129-137, verified) and its design right (local only, non-negative, 'zero for newcomers', no global aggregation — all confirmed) and then asserted that no serverless global ranking exists, two paragraphs away from the counterexample.
quantitative_errors: Successive Halving is cited with no bound, and the bound it has does not survive the roster. Karnin, Koren, Somekh (ICML 2013, PMLR 28(3):1238-1246 — bibliography confirmed) Theorem 4.1: Sequential Halving identifies the best arm with probability at least 1 - 3*log2(n)*exp(-T/(8*H2*log2(n))), i.e. T >= 8*H2*log2(n)*ln(3*log2(n)/delta). I computed this two ways (closed form and an mpmath root solve of the probability expression; both give 479.40228 for n=700, H2=1, delta=0.05). At the roster's upper bound of 700 seats: 10 rounds, and 479 graded observations even in the degenerate best case H2=1 (all gaps = 1 on a [0,1] score). With gaps of 0.2, H2 = 17,500 and T >= 8,389,540; with gaps of 0.1, H2 = 70,000 and T >= 33,558,160. A single-elimination knockout over 700 seats spends 699 matches. Invoking Successive Halving as the precedent that makes the ladder 'already invented' imports a guarantee the ladder's budget cannot buy, by four to five orders of magnitude.

The structural identification with Successive Halving is wrong in kind, not only in budget. Karnin's Algorithm 2 halves the ARM SET while doubling the SAMPLE COUNT on a FIXED stochastic arm whose mean does not change between rounds; the escalation is in measurement precision. The founder's ladder escalates DIFFICULTY, so each rung measures a different quantity, and the bound's i.i.d.-samples-from-a-stationary-per-arm-distribution assumption is simply absent. Jamieson and Talwalkar (AISTATS 2016, PMLR v51 — title and venue confirmed) handle the non-stochastic case only under an assumed convergent loss sequence with a uniform envelope, which a pass/fail rung at escalating difficulty does not provide. The dimension says the ladder 'is' Successive Halving. It is not: it is noisy tournament ranking with one observation per pairing, which has no guarantee at all.

'optimistic unchoking permanently reserves one upload slot in four' is implementation-specific and contradicted by the measurement paper the dimension also cites. Cohen 2003 says a peer 'unchokes a fixed number of other peers (default is four)' and separately 'has a single optimistic unchoke' — so 1 in 4 is a reading, not a stated figure, and 'permanently' is wrong twice over: the slot rotates 'every third rechoke period (30 seconds)', and anti-snubbing 'frequently results in more than one concurrent optimistic unchoke, (an exception to the exactly one optimistic unchoke rule)'. Piatek et al. measured the reference client at TWO optimistic unchoke slots: 'the reference BitTorrent client optimistically unchokes two peers every 30 seconds' and 'the number of optimistic unchoke slots defaults to 2'. If the founder is to borrow a reserved-exploration fraction, the number is 2 of the active set, not 1 in 4.

The 10-sample threshold is confirmed verbatim ('If the number of samples of R(H, V) exceeds a threshold (currently 10)') but its cost at this roster is never stated. At 700 seats, tier-1 measured estimates require 700 * 10 = 7,000 completed graded jobs PER TASK TYPE before any seat is routed on its own measurement; until then every seat sits on tier 2 or tier 3, i.e. on a population mean or a declared spec. Worse, the dimension recommends adopting quantile size-matching at the same time, which restricts each seat's sample to one size class — so the per-seat mean and the router become coupled, and the estimator no longer averages over the difficulty-estimation error the way random dispatch does. Neither the sample cost nor the coupling appears in the dimension.

The roster range 1 to 700 breaks the quantile machinery and the dimension does not address it. size_census computes effective speed as hav.et.avg * host.available_frac, sorts the population and finds quantile points (wiki text confirmed); with n = 1 the quantiles are undefined and with n in the tens the quantile assignment is dominated by sampling noise. BOINC's own figures are population-scale: 'throughput ... varies by two orders of magnitude in World Community Grid' (HICSS 4.5, verbatim). The dimension also confirms, correctly, that JobSizeMatching gives NO cold-start fallback for a host with no history — I re-checked the page and there is none.

Minor but worth correcting before it is quoted: the CPU/GPU efficiency figures come from two different sources and the dimension merges them. arXiv section 7 says only 'The efficiency of a CPU application can vary by a factor of 2 between computers' and 'The problem is worse for GPUs, for which efficiencies are typically much less than for CPUs, and vary more widely' — no percentages. The percentages are on the CreditNew wiki: 'very roughly, 10% for GPUs, 50% for CPUs'. Both halves of the dimension's sentence are true; they are not from the same place. The 'three credit systems' count is confirmed (the CreditNew page names 'The first credit system', 'The second credit system' and heads its proposal 'Goals of the new (third) credit system').

missed_mechanisms.name: HTCondor startd periodic benchmarking (Mips / KFlops ClassAd attributes)
missed_mechanisms.citation: HTCondor manual, EP policy configuration (htcondor.readthedocs.io/en/latest/admin-manual/ep-policy-configuration.html): 'The machine is running benchmarks to determine the speed on this machine', '...and perform benchmarks to determine Mips and KFlops', 'The startd automatically inserts an attribute, LastBenchmark, whenever it runs benchmarks', 'The startd keeps a weighted average of these benchmarking results', 'the startd will automatically run one set of benchmarks when it first starts up', and the documented default expression RunBenchmarks = (time() - LastBenchmark) >= (4 * $(HOUR)).
missed_mechanisms.why_it_matters: This is the founder's cold-start mechanism in its exact form AND it fixes the one breakage the dimension itself identifies in probe jobs. The dimension's complaint is that 'BOINC runs the probe ONCE and never again, so the resulting figure is a static snapshot — the founder's constraint that capability is measured, not assumed, is then only satisfied at t=0.' HTCondor runs the calibration task on first start and then re-runs it on a timer while the node is idle, keeps a weighted average rather than a snapshot, and stamps it with LastBenchmark so staleness is visible. It is a measured, persisted, continuously refreshed, name-free capability number consumed by the allocator. HTCondor is named in the dimension's own title and no HTCondor mechanism appears in the visible mechanism list.

missed_mechanisms.name: ClassAd bilateral matchmaking with two-sided Rank expressions
missed_mechanisms.citation: Raman, Livny and Solomon, 'Matchmaking: Distributed Resource Management for High Throughput Computing', IEEE HPDC '98, pp. 140-146, DOI 10.1109/hpdc.1998.709966 (also cited as [9] in the Anderson and Reed HICSS paper the dimension leans on).
missed_mechanisms.why_it_matters: It dissolves the dimension's fourth disagreement instead of conceding it. Matchmaking routes work by having each side publish Requirements and a Rank expression and pairing on mutual satisfaction, so allocation never needs a total order over the roster — each advertiser ranks only the offers in front of it. That is a far stronger answer to 'the founder may have a peer-to-peer CDSFL or a roster-wide measured capability ranking' than the Network of Favours, because it shows the roster-wide ranking is not the requirement in the first place; the requirement is a per-pairing preference. (Caveat to state plainly: HTCondor's negotiator is itself a central matchmaker, so ClassAds satisfy the no-total-order half, not the no-coordinator half.)

missed_mechanisms.name: EigenTrust / EigenRep — decentralised computation of a global reputation vector
missed_mechanisms.citation: Kamvar, Schlosser and Garcia-Molina, 'The EigenTrust algorithm for reputation management in P2P networks', WWW '03, p. 640, DOI 10.1145/775152.775242. Described in the Network of Favours paper itself: 'EigenRep [12] each peer stores local reputation values and in addition random peers store global values derived from multiple local values.'
missed_mechanisms.why_it_matters: It directly falsifies the first of the dimension's three 'NOT already invented' claims. EigenTrust produces exactly the artefact the dimension says has never been built — a roster-wide ordering with no coordinator — by distributed power iteration over locally held pairwise values, with score-manager replication for cheat resistance. Whether it suits CDSFL is a separate question (it needs pre-trusted peers to break symmetry and to resist collusion, which is itself a finding the founder should weigh), but the dimension cannot claim the thing does not exist.

missed_mechanisms.name: Gossip-based aggregation of network-wide order statistics
missed_mechanisms.citation: Jelasity, Montresor and Babaoglu, 'Gossip-based aggregation in large dynamic networks', ACM Transactions on Computer Systems 23(3):219-252, 2005, DOI 10.1145/1082469.1082470.
missed_mechanisms.why_it_matters: BOINC's size_census — sort the population, find the quantile points, hand them to the router — is the single most central operation in the whole dimension, and the dimension concedes it 'requires a population-wide census, which is a central-server operation'. Gossip aggregation computes means, variances, counts and quantiles over a dynamic population with no coordinator and O(log n) convergence. It is the missing bridge between the mechanism the dimension calls 'more useful to CDSFL than ranking is' and the founder's hard no-coordinator constraint, and its absence is why the dimension ends up declaring an impossibility instead of a design.

missed_mechanisms.name: BOINC client CPU benchmark (Whetstone) as the persisted capability prior
missed_mechanisms.citation: Anderson, arXiv:1903.01699, section 6.1: 'The client estimates the peak FLOPS of each instance. For CPUs this is the Whetstone benchmark result; for GPUs it's the vendor-supplied estimate based on number of cores and clock rate.' Credit history on the CreditNew wiki: 'The problem with this system is that, for a given app version, efficiency can vary widely between hosts', and 'It doesn't prevent credit cheating when single replication is used.'
missed_mechanisms.why_it_matters: This is the closest BOINC analogue to the founder's graded calibration task — run on every host, persisted, consumed downstream — and it is also the documented case study in why a single scalar capability number fails. Credit v1 was benchmark-times-time; it was abandoned because efficiency varies by host and because the benchmark was spoofable. That history is the strongest available evidence for the dimension's own third claim (no device-neutral, cheat-resistant single number exists) and it goes uncited, while the claim leans instead on an unsourceable quotation.

missed_mechanisms.name: Folding@home work-server assignment and the Quick Return Bonus; Einstein@Home
missed_mechanisms.citation: Named in the dimension's own title; no mechanism from either appears in the visible mechanism list. (I did not verify Folding@home's bonus formula within this task and am not asserting its details.)
missed_mechanisms.why_it_matters: Coverage gap against the dimension's stated scope rather than a substantive refutation. Folding@home's assignment-server model routes project classes by client capability and pays a return-speed bonus — a deadline-weighted incentive rather than a ranking — which is a third design point alongside BOINC's size matching and OurGrid's reciprocity. A specialist would expect at least one mechanism from each system named in the dimension title. Flagging it as unexamined rather than as established precedent, since the mechanism list was truncated mid-entry and may have contained more.

notes:
WHAT HOLDS. The citation record is unusually good for this kind of survey. I verified 36 of the dimension's claims against primary sources and most quotations are verbatim and correctly located. Confirmed exactly as claimed: HICSS section 4.9 probe jobs ("BOINC allows projects to provide 'probe jobs', which are executed exactly once on all hosts. The output of this job (typically an XML document) is stored in the host record in the database, and can be referenced in a project-specific scoring function"); HICSS 4.10 host punishment including the floor of 1 and recovery by doubling; the scoring term -(A-B)^2 in HICSS 4.8; "varies by two orders of magnitude in World Community Grid" in 4.5; proj_flops with the three tiers and "a threshold (currently 10)" in arXiv section 6.3; "some computers are reliable for CPU jobs but unreliable for GPU jobs" in section 3.4; "A job that completes in five minutes on one could take a week on the other" and "it's desirable that job runtime be on the order of an hour" in section 3.5; the size_census / quantile / size_regulator machinery and the absence of any cold-start fallback on the JobSizeMatching wiki; Sarmenta FGCS 18(4):561-572; Paranhos Euro-Par 2003 pp. 169-180; Network of Favours HPDC-13 2004 pp. 129-137 with local-only non-negative reputation and no global aggregation; Karnin ICML 2013 PMLR 28(3):1238-1246; Jamieson and Talwalkar AISTATS 2016; Kondo SC '04 PRI-HISTORY's poor performance, the non-stationarity across weekdays, the 110-minute and 108-minute errors against tasks "less then 2 hours in length", and the left-heavy clock-rate distribution; the Journal of Grid Computing pagination 5:379-405; three of four Estrada claims; and "Volunteer computing uses central servers. There is typically no peer-to-peer communication" on the BOINC VolunteerComputing wiki.

THE ONE SOURCING ITEM THE FOUNDER MUST NOT QUOTE YET. "CreditNew is complicated and I'm not sure it ever worked exactly as I intended" has no citation in the dimension and I could not locate it in the CreditNew wiki, arXiv:1903.01699 or the HICSS paper. My web-search budget was exhausted (the limit is shared across all agents in this turn) before I could check BOINC message-board and mailing-list archives, so I am not calling it fabricated — I am calling it unverified. It is one of three pillars of the "not already invented" verdict, so it needs a URL or it needs removing.

THE SHARPEST SUBSTANTIVE DEFECT — THE "FIRST, AND MOST SERIOUS" DISAGREEMENT IS NOT ABOUT CAPABILITY. The dimension says Kondo et al. "built exactly the founder's mechanism — PRI-HISTORY, which predicts each host's future throughput from measured past performance" and that it shows "measured capability history can be WORSE than a cheap static attribute". The paper's own definition refutes that reading: "The method PRI-HISTORY uses a history of a host's past performance to predict its future performance. Specifically, for each host, the scheduler calculates the expected operations per availability interval (that is how many operations can be executed in between two host failures) using the previous weekday's trace." What is predicted is the AVAILABILITY INTERVAL — how long the machine stays up between failures — and what was measured as non-stationary is availability: "the availability interval size, both in terms of time and in terms of operations, was not stationary across weekdays." Within each of PRI-HISTORY's two priority queues, hosts are then ordered by speed anyway. And the thing that beat it, clock rate, IS a capability measure — just a declared one. So the finding is: a churn forecast from yesterday's trace does not survive to today, therefore do not route on predicted uptime. It is not: a measured capability number is worse than a declared one. CDSFL seats do not churn the way a 2004 enterprise desktop did, and the founder's calibration task grades reasoning quality, not uptime. The precondition the dimension derives ("measurement pays only when capability is stationary over a horizon longer than one task") is a reasonable generalisation and worth keeping — but it must be presented as an extrapolation from an availability result, not as a measured refutation of capability measurement. Note too that the transfer the dimension endorses points at routing by the spec sheet, which the founder has ruled out as a hard constraint; the dimension does not flag that its own preferred option breaks one.

THE STRUCTURAL DEFECT. Five mechanisms are labelled DIRECTLY_APPLICABLE and all five are central-server mechanisms, under a constraint set that includes "must work with no central coordinator". The dimension knows this — its fourth disagreement says so — and then leaves the labels standing. The honest shape is: BOINC has solved the heterogeneity problem and the never-set-aside problem comprehensively, FOR A STAR TOPOLOGY, and every one of those solutions has to be re-derived for a coordinator-free roster. Two of the missed mechanisms above (gossip aggregation for the census, ClassAd two-sided Rank for routing without a total order) are the route to doing that, and both were available to a specialist in this exact field.

TWO QUOTE-MINING ERRORS, BOTH REVERSING THE SOURCE. Piatek's low-bandwidth sentence is followed immediately by the finding that low-capacity peers are over-served through indiscriminate optimistic unchokes; the dimension's warning that the small-model end will be starved is the inverse of the measurement. SETI@home's work-unit enlargement was a redundancy-control move, not a heterogeneity response. Both quotes are real. Both arguments built on them are not.

WHAT I COULD NOT FULLY VERIFY. The SC '04 full text is paywalled (DOI 10.1109/SC.2004.50 confirmed, abstract elided by the publisher); I worked from a pdftotext extraction already present in the shared scratchpad, whose artefacts (column interleaving, "PRI-CRWAIT" hyphen breaks) are consistent with a genuine extraction, and every bibliographic field I could check independently matched. The journal abstract and the Estrada e-Science '06 venue string were likewise not independently re-fetched. Treat the Kondo and Estrada quotations as high-confidence but second-hand within this verification.
